title: On‑Prem K8s Ignite Sequence: Fastpath Install Playbook for BareMetal + vSphere
body:
Purpose:
This playbook defines a minimal, repeatable "ignite" sequence to bootstrap an on‑prem Kubernetes cluster in two common footprints: bare‑metal (PXE/IPXE -> Ignition/Cloud‑Init) and vSphere (OVF/Template -> cloud‑init). The goal is a predictable fastpath for initial install, with Terraform module notes and an upgrade plan for patch and minor upgrades. This is a working doc: keep it short and pragmatic — checklists, commands, and failure modes.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target: Kubernetes 1.26+ (tune for 1.27/1.28 as needed)
- Control plane HA = 3 nodes (or 1 for PoC); worker pool separate by class (gpu/cpu/edge)
- Network: BGP or routed VLANs (we assume routed VLANs by default)
- Storage: local SSD + optional Ceph or NFS for persistent volumes
- Airgap? Separate notes below.
- Terraform is used for provisioning VMs/IPAM and generating Ignition/cloud‑init assets; installer (kubeadm or MCO) will be invoked post‑boot.

Goals and success criteria:
- Fresh cluster reachable (kube‑api responding) within expected SLO: 20–40 minutes for vSphere templates, 40–90 minutes for baremetal PXE path (depending on image size, network boot speed).
- Nodes join and are Ready; kube‑system pods (coredns, kube-proxy, calico/flannel) are Running; control plane certificate validity and kubeconfig accessible.
- Zero manual VM/container networking edits after template/ignition generation.

Preflight checklist (must pass before proceed):
- IPAM blocks reserved for control-plane and workers; DNS entries for api.<cluster> and lb.<cluster> created
- Load balancer method: HAProxy/MetalLB for bare‑metal or vSphere LB for templates configured
- SSH keys, KMS secrets (ETCD encryption key) present in secrets manager
- Terraform state backend configured (s3/minio, GCS), locking enabled
- Images validated sha256 (image manifest + signature if available)
- Node firmware/drivers verified (NIC offload settings, NVMe/RAID config)

Fastpath sequence (high level):
1) Generate install assets with Terraform
   - terraform apply generates: ignition/cloud‑init blobs, kubeadm-config.yaml, kubeadm init manifest, kubeconfig bootstrap token, haproxy config or metalLB manifest, and cloud networking userdata
   - Output artifacts placed in an ephemeral object store (S3 path) or uploaded to templates in vCenter

2) Provision compute resources
   - vSphere: clone template -> inject cloud‑init -> power on
   - Baremetal: write iPXE scripts, point DHCP option 67 to HTTP server with Ignition; power on nodes

3) Control plane bootstrap
   - First control node boots, executes cloud‑init -> runs kubeadm init --config=/etc/kubeadm/kubeadm-config.yaml
   - Wait for kube-apiserver to be Up; apply CNI manifest and core addons from the bootstrap host
   - After CNI Ready, kubeadm join tokens used by remaining control nodes; apply LB and add other control nodes

4) Workers join and label pools
   - Worker bootstraps with join token; terraform outputs node join command as template
   - After Ready, run node‑pools labeling and taints (gpu=true, workload=edge, etc.)

5) Post‑bootstrap validations (smoke tests)
   - kubectl get cs && kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l matches expected
   - Sample workloads scheduled across pools, exec into pods to check DNS (nslookup kube-dns)
   - Latency baseline: kube-apiserver p95 under target; ping between nodes for MTU and routing verification

Important Terraform module notes (practical guidance):
- Module layout: 
  - modules/compute/vsphere (inputs: template_name, resource_pool, datacenter, network_map, customization_spec; outputs: vm_ids, ip_addresses)
  - modules/compute/baremetal (inputs: mac_list, iPXE_http_base, ignition_blob_paths; outputs: mac->ip map, provisioning_job_ids)
  - modules/network (inputs: vlan_ids, subnet_cidrs, dhcp_ranges, lb_endpoints; outputs: dns_records)
  - modules/bootstrap (inputs: kube_version, kubeadm_config_template, etcd_encrypt_key; outputs: kubeconfig_path, bootstrap_token)
- Patterns: keep Ignition/cloud‑init content generated and stored as templates in the terraform state (do not commit full secrets); reference by object storage URL.
- Idempotency: modules should return a checksum for rendered ignition blobs; terraform compares checksum to avoid reupload on small edits.
- Secrets handling: use KMS envelope encryption for ETCD key and cloud‑init sensitive sections; use terraform provider that supports sealed secrets in object storage.
- Versioning: attach cluster and module version tags to vSphere templates and baremetal images; terraform should refuse to deploy if image major version mismatch unless force flag used.

Ignition / cloud‑init best practices (differences callout):
- Baremetal (Ignition): use Ignition to create kubelet unit, drop kubeadm config, and run kubeadm; smaller on‑disk images reduce boot time
- vSphere (cloud‑init): customize via guest‑customization or cloud‑init user data; prefer cloud‑init to run minimal post‑install and then download kubeadm config from secure store
- Both: do not bake join tokens in images; token created per run and stored in state with TTL 2h by default

Upgrade plan (patch and minor):
- Patch (1.26.x -> 1.26.y) – fast path (automated):
  1. Run clusterwide smoke test baseline and record kubelet and control plane versions
  2. Upgrade control plane one node at a time: cordon -> drain (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data) -> upgrade kubeadm / kubelet -> kubeadm upgrade apply on control node -> uncordon -> wait for Ready
  3. When all control nodes pass, upgrade workers in rolling batches (maxUnavailable 10–25%) by draining and upgrading kubelet+cri and kubeadm; verify workloads reschedule
- Minor (1.26 -> 1.27) – staged with canary and validation:
  1. Create a canary cluster (or new control-plane replica set) using same terraform modules but target new k8s version; run e2e regression against core features and Redwood-specific workloads (prefix cache, kv cache behavior)
  2. If canary passes, perform control plane upgrade per pod‑disruption budget strategy: canary control node -> remaining control nodes -> workers
  3. Monitor telemetry (API error rates, latency, token bucket overflows) for 48–72 hours after upgrade

Rollback strategy:
- Control plane: kubeadm supports rollback for certain components only. Plan to snapshot ETCD before control plane upgrades (etcdctl snapshot save), and keep a tested restore path.
- Worker node failure: reprovision from image/template and rejoin (terraform destroy/create or node reprovision job).
- Full cluster major failure: restore ETCD to a new control plane cluster created from previous template and kubeadm configs. Document recovery runbook as separate play.

Validation and automation hooks (CI):
- terraform plan output must include artifact checksums + image tags; CI gate prevents apply if signature missing
- E2E job: small smoke harness that runs after bootstrap, validates basic Redwood inference components (rediscovery of model cache, KV warmup)
- Canary post‑upgrade run: traffic routed to canary models for 10% traffic and regressions checked against golden prompts

Airgap considerations (short notes):
- All artifacts (images, oci blobs, kubeadm binaries, CNI manifests) must be mirrored to internal registry and image manifest pinned
- Ignition/cloud‑init blobs reference internal artifact store only; no external URLs

Common failure modes and quick troubleshooting:
- PXE/IPXE stalls at iPXE prompt: check DHCP option 67/66, verify HTTP file server path, confirm MTU and jumbo frame settings
- Node boots but never Ready: docker/containerd failing due to cgroup mismatch; check kernel args (systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0 vs 1) and CRI config
- CNI pods CrashLoopBackoff: wrong MTU or missing backend IPIP/VXLAN setting; apply debug image and test pod-to-pod ping
- kube‑apiserver cert issues after time skew: ensure NTP/chrony set in cloud‑init; if certs invalid, rotate using kubeadm certs renew

Quick commands bundle (to keep in runbook):
- terraform workspace select <cluster>; terraform plan -var-file=secrets.tfvars
- ssh into bootstrap node: journalctl -u kubelet -f; sudo kubeadm init phase control-plane all --config /etc/kubeadm/kubeadm-config.yaml
- token create: kubeadm token create --print-join-command --ttl 2h
- etcd snapshot: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-$(date +%s).db --endpoints=https://localhost:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.key

Post-install housekeeping:
- Register vCenter templates/images with version metadata
- Export terraform state snapshot and store in secure blob for recovery exercises
- Add cluster to Redwood Console observability (token, endpoint, team mapping)

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide on default LB for baremetal: MetalLB vs external HAProxy appliance — performance tests pending (INF-4783)
- Formalize image signing process for appliances (cos, ubuntu) and integrate into terraform CI
- Automation to rotate kubeadm bootstrap tokens and reduce human intervention in long-lived clusters

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep the ignition blobs small; offload large artifacts to local registry to speed boot
- Try a 2‑stage rollout in lab: vSphere template + baremetal ipxe to validate edge cases

References and attachments:
- internal mirror: s3://redwood-infra-artifacts/onprem/ignite/<cluster>/
- PR with terraform modules: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-provisioning/pull/612

End of playbook — ping me (Ava) if you want this converted into a checklist template or a stepper script that operators can run from laptop.
